titre: Saint-Pierre, 1902: It Wasn't the Lava That Killed
accroche: On May 8, 1902, Mount Pelée destroys Saint-Pierre in a few minutes. The culprit is a cloud of gas and ash, not a lava flow.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 8, 1902, around 8 a.m., Mount Pelée explodes above Saint-Pierre, in Martinique. The telegraph line is cut at 7:52 a.m.; the blast reaches the city around 8:02. Almost all of the city's roughly 28,000 inhabitants die, and estimates of the total toll range from 28,000 to 40,000 dead depending on the source. One readily imagines a city buried under lava. That is inaccurate: a lava dome about 300 meters high formed at the summit only from October 1902 to September 1903.

## A Cloud, Not a Flow

What destroys the city is a flow of scorching gas, ash, and blocks, which we now call a pyroclastic flow. According to a later calculation, it raced down the slope at more than 160 kilometers per hour. The geologist Alfred Lacroix, sent on a mission to the Antilles in 1902-1903, introduces the term *nuée ardente* (“glowing cloud”) to describe it. He photographs one on December 16, 1902, and in 1904 publishes a landmark work, *La Montagne Pelée et ses éruptions* (Mount Pelée and Its Eruptions). The type of eruption he describes has since borne the name of the volcano: we speak of a Peléan eruption.

## A Volcano Believed Extinct

The mountain had been thought extinct since 1767. Its explosions resume in April 1902. On May 5, the failure of a natural dam that held back the crater lake releases a mudflow that kills about 150 people. Yet a local commission reassures the population: the mountain would present no more danger to Saint-Pierre than Vesuvius does to Naples. The city is destroyed about 24 hours later. On May 20, a new eruption kills about 2,000 people, including rescuers and sailors.

## The Legend of the Two Survivors

A second received idea concerns the survivors. The legend counts two: a prisoner, locked in a windowless cell, and a cobbler from the outskirts, Léon Compère-Léandre. Recent sources judge it false: a number of people survived on the edge of the devastated zone, often severely burned, and several died afterward, without their names being recorded. The prisoner himself goes by two names depending on the text: Louis-Auguste Cyparis or Ludger Sylbaris. A ten-year-old girl, Havivra Da Ifrile, is said to have reached a cave by boat before being picked up at sea.

All of this does not make the catastrophe any gentler, only better described. Without Lacroix's mission, the name of the thing might still be missing: Mount Pelée led, as early as 1903, to the founding of the Martinique volcanological and seismological observatory, the second in the world after the one at Vesuvius, created in 1841.

repere.texte: At Saint-Pierre, on May 8, 1902, about 28,000 inhabitants are killed by a nuée ardente. Pelée's lava dome, about 300 m high, forms only from October 1902 to September 1903.
repere.source: Scientific American, “May 8, 1902: La Pelée” (History of Geology); Wikipedia, “1902 eruption of Mount Pelée”

carte.punch: Saint-Pierre was not buried under lava: a cloud of scorching gas destroyed it in 1902.
carte.idee: On May 8, 1902, Pelée destroys Saint-Pierre with a flow of gas, ash, and blocks, which Lacroix names “nuée ardente.” The lava dome only forms starting in October 1902. And the survivors numbered more than two.

quiz.question: What destroyed Saint-Pierre on May 8, 1902?
choix: A lava flow more fluid than usual, which reached the city in a few minutes
A tsunami triggered by the volcano collapsing into the sea
A mudflow from the crater lake, like the one on May 5
A flow of scorching gas, ash, and blocks that raced down the slope at high speed
quiz.explication: On May 8, it is a nuée ardente, a pyroclastic flow, that strikes the city. The May 5 mudflow killed about 150 people, not the city's 28,000. The lava dome only appears starting in October 1902, and no tsunami is involved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When did Pelée's lava dome form?
choix: Before May 8, 1902, which explains the city's destruction
From October 1902 to September 1903, that is, after the city's destruction
It never formed, contrary to a received idea
In a single night, on May 8, 1902
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The lava dome, about 300 meters high, only forms between October 1902 and September 1903, long after the city's destruction on May 8, and is therefore not the cause of the catastrophe.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who introduced the term nuée ardente to describe this type of eruption?
choix: Professor Landes, author of the report that had judged the mountain harmless to the city
The cobbler Léon Compère-Léandre, one of the few survivors of the catastrophe
The geologist Alfred Lacroix, sent on a mission to the Antilles in 1902-1903
An engineer from the Vesuvius observatory, sent as reinforcement from Italy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Alfred Lacroix, a geologist sent on a mission to the Antilles in 1902-1903, who introduces the term nuée ardente; he photographs one on December 16, 1902 and publishes the landmark work in 1904.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened on May 5, 1902, three days before the destruction of Saint-Pierre?
choix: A first nuée ardente reached the city's outskirts without causing any casualties
The city was entirely evacuated on the governor's orders
The lava dome appeared at the volcano's summit for the first time
The failure of a natural dam released a mudflow from the crater lake, killing about 150 people
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On May 5, the failure of the dam holding back the crater lake releases a mudflow that kills about 150 people, a toll far lower than that of May 8 and unrelated to the dome, which only appeared starting in October.
